decisions.detail: QUOTE: Unless `MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS` is defined, it expands to `private_##member`, so the public struct field is really named `private_member`. ... Inside the library, `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(x)` is just `x`. | WHY: The answer states the default rename to private_<member> and that defining the opt-in leaves the member name unchanged.

decisions.mark: explains that the two branches give different consumers different views — code that defines MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS sees plain member names while an ordinary consumer of the public headers sees the renamed ones
decisions.detail: QUOTE: Unless `MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS` is defined, it expands to `private_##member`, so the public struct field is really named `private_member`. ... Inside the library, `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(x)` is just `x`. | WHY: The answer says that code defining the opt-in (the library, some programs) gets plain names, while ordinary consumers of the public headers get `private_` names, and that two translation units compiled with different settings "see different field names". || QUOTE: Unless `MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS` is defined, it expands to `private_##member`, so the public struct field is really named `private_member`. ... Inside the library, `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(x)` is just `x`. | WHY: The answer states that the macro expands differently depending on whether the opt-in is defined (library and opted-in programs get plain names, other consumers get `private_` names). || QUOTE: Unless `MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS` is defined, it expands to `private_##member`, so the public struct field is really named `private_member`. ... Inside the library, `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(x)` is just `x`. | WHY: The answer explains that the macro renames fields to `private_member` for ordinary consumers, while code that defines the opt-in (the library, some programs) sees plain names.

decisions.mark: concludes that this enforces API opacity at COMPILE time by breaking the member name, rather than by hiding the struct layout — the fields remain visible and sized
decisions.detail: QUOTE: "it expands to `private_##member`, so the public struct field is really named `private_member`. Code that writes `ctx->state` by its plain name fails to compile." and "The macro only renames fields, so struct layout is identical whether or not the opt-in is on." | WHY: The answer states opacity is enforced at compile time via renaming the member, with layout unchanged (fields still present and sized). || QUOTE: "It is a source-level guard, not a runtime or ABI mechanism. The macro only renames fields, so struct layout is identical whether or not the opt-in is on." | WHY: The answer says that opacity comes from renaming the fields at compile time (`private_##member`) and that the struct layout is unchanged, so the fields stay visible and sized. || QUOTE: It is a source-level guard, not a runtime or ABI mechanism. The macro only renames fields, so struct layout is identical whether or not the opt-in is on. | WHY: The answer says that opacity is enforced at compile time by renaming fields to private_member, and that the struct layout is unchanged, so the fields stay visible and sized.

Inside the library, `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(x)` is just `x`. | WHY: The answer states that library/common.h defines the opt-out and that every library .c includes it first, so library code sees plain member names.
